message.content:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler, written in Rust), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Your part: the project-settings and drafting-style commands that edit the project's library sections: `line_pattern`, `line_style`, `fill_pattern`, `import_fill_patterns`, `export_fill_patterns`, `filled_region_type`, `text_type`, `dimension_type`, `line_weights`, `object_styles`, `units`, `room_area`, `language`, `standard`, `phase`, `phase_filter`, `option`, `parameter`, `voltage`, `distribution_system`, `wire_type`, `reinforcement_preset`.

## Hard rules (violating any of these fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it. NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace it or try to read it. Never modify or delete it. NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet. Do not look for the program's source anywhere.
- Rust standard library only. Your code goes in `src/styles/` (submodules as you like). Avoid editing other files; if you must, keep it minimal and say so.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repository, e.g. `/tmp/styles-agent/`. Commit only Rust.

## The codebase (read first)
You are in a git worktree of the repo. `src/json.rs` (JSON `Value`, insertion-ordered `Map` with `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like sections, serde_json-identical parse errors and float formatting incl. `1e+16`; `.sorted()` — command replies are printed sorted), `src/project.rs` (`Project`: `doc` Map of top-level sections in file order with `insert_top`/`section_mut`; `TOP_ORDER` is a guess — correct the places of the sections you add (e.g. `phases`, `phase_filters`, `option_sets`, `line_weights`, `object_styles`, `room_area`, `standard`, `reinforcement_presets`…) by observing saved files; `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` of `{kind, name, guid}` entries with `lib_add`/`lib_find`/…, ids counting down from 999999 via `alloc_lib_id`), `src/session.rs` (`execute` snapshots, runs, runs `crate::check::check`, rolls back on error, undo history labelled by the command's label), `src/commands/params.rs` (helpers producing the original's error texts: extend with new ones in your module), `src/model.rs`. The default project (`/workspace/executable run --save x.bimcraft`) shows the sections you edit (line_patterns, line_styles, fill_patterns, region_types, text_types, dimension_types, voltages, distribution_systems, wire_types, parameters, view_templates) and the library entries naming them. Your entry points exist in `src/styles/mod.rs`: `dispatch(s, cid, p)` and `check(pr)`. Build: `cargo build --release` in your worktree.

## Documentation
The entries for your commands in `/workspace/executable commands` (their parameter descriptions are the spec), and `/workspace/README.md` (grep: Line Weights, Object Styles, Line Styles, line pattern, fill pattern, PAT, phase, design option, project parameter, Electrical Settings, reinforcement_preset, standard), `/workspace/docs/areas/phasing.md`, `/workspace/docs/areas/views-and-graphics.md` and `/workspace/docs/areas/structure-and-mep.md` for the parts that concern you.

## Targets (the hidden tests compare the original and your program exactly, after GUIDs are renumbered by first appearance)
For each command: the reply (listing, create, change, rename, delete), every error text, what the saved project file holds (`--save x.bimcraft`), and the undo label. A known test expects `export_fill_patterns {"path": "out.pat", "names": ["Brick 225 x 75", "Café tiles", "Plain"]}` after making two patterns to write exactly `/workspace/assets/test_drawing_fills/out.pat`; PAT import/export (units, `;%TYPE=`, number formatting, what's left out and why) must match the original on many PAT texts you write. `phase`/`phase_filter`/`option` also show in `inspect` (phases, phase_filters, phase_overrides, option_sets) — note what `inspect` must print; inspect itself is someone else's. Where a command depends on elements (e.g. renaming a phase that elements use via `params`, deleting a line style that detail lines use, a parameter's values on elements), handle the library side and note what else is needed.

## Testing tool
`MINE=<worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] -- <args…>` runs both programs in fresh temp dirs and diffs normalised exit code, stdout, stderr and all files written (SAME or a diff). Example: `... -- run --cmd 'line_style {"name":"Red","pen":3,"color":"#ff0000"}' --save x.bimcraft`.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch. Final message: branch and commit, per command what matches and what doesn't, and what the core must provide (inspect keys, element-side updates).

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

content.content:
240 | Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable
tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and
steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says
(an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each
type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray),
`IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and `IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may
read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`,
`distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in
mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |
-----
243 | Reinforcement | `rebar` makes reinforcing bars: a round bar of a diameter (3 to 100 mm) and a steel grade (CA-50 unless told) bent along points in mm, in the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces, which it goes
with; `closed` makes a hoop, and `count` with `step` a layer of bars or hoops along a beam. A schedule of rebar lists grade, diameter, length, count and weight (steel at 7850 kg/m³) and, grouped, is a bar schedule. IFC
writes and reads each as an `IfcReinforcingBar`, aggregated to its host. The 3D view draws them as tubes (inside their host, so hide it to see them), a section draws the bars it cuts as dots over the poché, and a plan
draws each bar of its level as a thin line (solid under the cut plane, dashed over it and under the view range's top, a bar that stands as a dot, bars lying on one another drawn once), hidden with the category.
`reinforce` arms a beam, a column, a footing or a floor (round columns and footings, and sloped floors, too) by rules: the engineer gives the cover (or the host's `Cobrimento` parameter) and how many bars, how thick and
how far apart (a beam's bars below and above, stirrups with closer ends and hooks, skin bars and anchors; a column's bars on each face, stirrups and ties; a footing's two layers of mesh with their ends turned up; a
floor's meshes below and above, stopping short of its outline and openings), and it lays them out inside the cover, checks they fit with room between them and says what to change; a beam's bars and a column's end in
hooks if told, some of a beam's bottom bars bend up at each end to the top at an angle (`bent`) and a column's bars step in toward its axis near the top (`jog`); each bar is on a layer, and reinforcing again replaces
what it made and leaves bars drawn by hand. `hosts` arms a list alike, all or none (up to 1000 hosts and 20000 bars), and `reinforcement_preset` keeps a named set of the parameters for a kind of host in the project,
which `reinforce` takes with `preset` and lets what is given replace. The numbers are the engineer's; `check` "NBR 6118" (with the aggressiveness class and `fck`) adds notes, never a refusal, where the bars made fall
short of its usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars), typed from public handbooks and not from the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. On the
desktop, the Structure tab's Reinforce (RF) opens a dialog for the elements selected (any number, of one kind), with the fields of their kind, saying a refusal inside itself, keeping what was typed for the next of its
kind, saving the fields as a preset to choose for another and deleting one, and with Remove Bars for the bars it made. Not yet: bends other than a hook, a bent-up bar and a column's jog, round beams, bars beyond a
section's cut seen through the concrete. |
-----
249 | Views | A floor plan per level with Revit's view range: cut at its cut plane (1200 mm up by default), what lies below seen from it down to the bottom, faint beyond it down to the view depth, and roofs overhead up to
the top: wall poché with clean joins at any angle, compound walls' layers, hatched with their materials' cut patterns where they're wide enough (else lighter where they aren't structure), door swings, window glass, room
tags, grid bubbles, dimensions, door and window tags; PNG and SVG, which letter the view's name at the plan's bottom left (the window letters it too, over the canvas and on the screen only, which File > Settings can
hide; a viewport on a sheet has its own title). Sections and elevations along any line: the cut in poché (a roof's along its slope, a compound wall's, floor's, roof's or ceiling's with its layers), what lies beyond in
hidden line, levels named with their heights, grids; the four building elevations in one go; their marks on every plan; PNG. Crop regions on plans and sections: the view shows only what's inside, grids stopping at its
edge with their bubbles. A reflected ceiling plan per level: its walls cut at 2300 mm (over the doors, through the windows), looking up at the ceilings, their tiles and the shafts through them, and at the beams and
columns over the cut up to the ceilings, in projection (one over a ceiling is hidden by it). A 3D view, from any angle: walls with their doors and windows cut out, slabs and ceilings with their shafts cut out, columns,
stairs and roofs, door leaves and glass, shaded (each layer in its material's colour), with an edge wherever faces meet, but none between the facets of a curve (a curved wall's, a round form's, an imported mesh's where
its triangles turn less than 20°), which shades smoothly across them; PNG. A plan or a section always has a scale, 1 : n (1 : 100, or 1/8" = 1'-0" in feet and inches, until set): it stands for paper at that scale, and
its annotation (lettering, grid bubbles, marks, dimension ticks) and its line weights are that paper's, so on screen a line is as thick as it would print at the zoom (at least a pixel; Thin Lines draws all of them one).
A line weight is a pen, 1 to 16, or 0, a hairline, the thinnest line the screen, a PNG or a printer draws, at any scale and zoom; what pens 1 to 16 draw is the project's Line Weights (Manage > Line Weights, as Revit's):
the model's pens at each of a list of scales, a view taking the nearest scale's, and the annotation's (dimensions, tags, text, grids, levels, marks) at any scale, edited by scale, added and deleted, applied as one undo
step and saved with the project. Which pen each model category draws its own lines in, cut and seen, is the project's Object Styles (Manage > Object Styles, as Revit's), in every plan and section, a view's
Visibility/Graphics over them. Detail lines draw in one view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet) in a line style: a pen, a colour and a line pattern, its freely ordered gaps, straight strokes, dots, centered
parallel offsets, waves, zigzags and text in mm on paper so it reads the same at any scale; the Line Pattern Creator previews straight or curved paths and letters text with bundled IBM Plex Sans, while geometry and
dimensions keep the centerline (Manage > Line Styles, styles and patterns made, changed, renamed and deleted as one undo step; a project starts with Thin, Medium and Wide Lines, a Hairline, Hidden, Centre and Overhead
Lines). A cut wall's outline is inked over its poché, and not across where walls join. A plan or a section has a detail level too: coarse (what it cuts in one poché, an opening as its gap and jambs), medium (a compound
element's layers and an opening's leaf, swing and glass) or fine, as it has always drawn (the layers' patterns too); the 3D view has a visual style: shaded, hidden line (paper-white faces with their edges, what a face
hides staying hidden) or wireframe (every edge, seen through the faces). A viewport takes its view's scale; a sheet keeps annotation at paper size. A view fitted into an image (a PNG, Zoom to Fit) leaves as much room
round it as its annotation takes at its scale, which grows with the scale, so 1 : 500 doesn't cut its grid bubbles or level names off. A level can have more plans than its own, as Revit's Duplicate View makes them
(`duplicate_view`, DP): each a plan view with its own view range, crop and graphics and its own dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations over the same model; with detailing it starts with its source's annotation; a
dependent view follows its parent's view range and graphics (scale and detail too), has a crop of its own, and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. They go on sheets, take view templates and have ceiling
plans as levels do. Sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet. The 3D view is parallel (axonometric) or in perspective, as through a camera: picked from Projection in its Properties
(or `perspective`), seen through a lens of a focal length typed there, from an eye raised or lowered to a height typed there, and orbited, panned, zoomed, picked and edited as ever, on the processor or the graphics card.
The Camera tool (`camera`) makes a view of its own, as Revit's does: an eye and a target are clicked in a plan (each at a height over it, typed in the Options Bar), and a named 3D view in perspective opens looking from
the eye at the target; it is listed under 3D Views in the Project Browser, opens from its own camera, and its name, eye, target and lens are read and changed in Properties, whether it is open or its mark on the plan is
picked (`camera` reads or changes one too, by name or id; a view with no camera shows the azimuth and elevation it is framed by on a sheet instead). The camera shows on its level's plan as a mark at its eye with a line
to what it looks at: it is picked there and opened by its right-click menu (or a double click), and its eye and target follow the mouse as the view is orbited, panned or zoomed, so leaving the view and coming back stands
it where it was left. The 3D view has a section box, as Revit's: six planes square to the axes that keep what lies between them, the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, turned on and off with BX or its
Properties, each face dragged by its grip in the view or typed in Properties, its extents kept while it's off; the levels it doesn't reach are left out. A plan can follow it (Section Box in the plan's Properties): it
then shows what the box keeps, cut at the box's top, seen down to its bottom and cropped to its sides, and snaps to a scan where the box's top cuts it |
-----
252 | Visibility and graphics | What each view hides, and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does, for each plan, section, elevation and 3D view: whole categories left out (walls, doors, rooms, grids,
dimensions, levels in a section…), or single elements; lines and fills overridden by category, by element and by view filter: a colour, weight and dash for what the view cuts and for what it sees (a plan's below its cut
plane, the annotation; in 3D, and in a section beyond its line, the edges' colour), the cut's poché colour or a 3D view's surface colour (a weight is a pen, 0 a hairline at any scale), halftone (halfway to the paper)
and, in 3D, transparency, where what lies behind shows through and a click still picks the element (halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can't take its category's away). A hidden door or window
leaves its opening in the wall, and snaps, Tag All, Select All and a view's framing take what it shows. View filters pick elements out by rules, a schedule filter's (a field of the category, how to compare it, a value,
project parameters among the fields), on the categories chosen; a view applies them in order, the first prevailing where they disagree, and one that hides hides whatever the others say; an element's own override beats
the filters', and those beat the category's. View templates keep a view's categories, filters, phase, design options, scale, detail level, visual style and, for a plan, view range under a name, for other views to follow:
what a template controls isn't the view's to change, and changed, every view following it follows. A project's filters and templates are saved with it; sheets print each view as its graphics say |
-----
253 | Phasing and design options | Phases in order, as Revit's Phasing has them (a project starts with Existing and New Construction): each element is made in one (its `Phase Created`, the first unless it says) and may be
taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), so in a view's phase it is new, existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (made and taken down in it), and what is made after the phase, or taken down before it,
isn't there. A view has a phase (the project's last unless it says) and a phase filter, which shows each status as its category does, as the project's overrides for that status say (existing in halftone and demolished
dashed red to begin with, both yours to change) or not at all; a project starts with Show All, Show Complete, Show New, Show Previous + Demolished and Show Previous + New. A door or window with no phase of its own
follows its wall. Phases are added, inserted, renamed and combined, and what was made, taken down or shown in one goes along; phase filters are made and changed. Design options are sets of options, as Revit's Design
Options: an element in an option of a set (`Design Option`, `set: option`) shows only in a view that shows that option, the set's primary unless the view chooses, and one in none shows everywhere. Options are added,
renamed, made the primary and taken out (one with elements in it stays until they are moved); accepting the primary keeps its elements and takes the others' and the set away, and deleting a set takes its elements too.
What a session makes is made in the phase of the view it is drawn in, when that view has a phase or a phase filter of its own, and in the active design option; a copy is made in them too, and isn't taken down with the
element it was copied from, while what is made with a phase or an option given keeps it. Schedules and view filters read the phase and the option as fields (a schedule sorts and groups the phases in the project's order,
Existing before New Construction, whatever their names; a rule that names a phase, an option or a set follows it when it is renamed or combined); the desktop's Demolish tool (DW) takes an element down in the phase of the
view it is clicked in, and a second click takes it back; templates can control a view's phase and its options; sheets print each view in its phase; a project's phases, filters, overrides and sets are saved with it. A
project saved before phases that holds a project parameter named `Phase Created`, `Phase Demolished` or `Design Option` opens with it renamed (`Phase Created Parameter`), its values with it |
-----
256 | Project parameters | Values of your own that each element of their categories holds (text, numbers, lengths, yes or no, unset a no), as Revit's project parameters are: set in Properties or with `modify`, shown,
filtered and sorted in schedules and read by their formulas, and written to IFC in a `Project Parameters` property set and read back from it; renamed, schedules follow; taken off a category, its elements and schedules
lose them |
-----
263 | Files | `.bimcraft` projects (JSON, file format 12: every save is 12, so an earlier build refuses even a plain project saved by this one, saying it is from a newer BIMCraft); IFC4 export with storeys, walls swept up
from their plan outline (mitred where they join, an arc in short chords) or, attached to a roof, as closed shells, walls, floors, roofs and ceilings with their material layer sets (each material with its colour), slabs
(sloped ones as closed shells), ceilings as coverings, spaces and columns, walls, slabs, doors and windows with their `Qto_*BaseQuantities` (a wall's side area and volume gross and less its openings, a slab's area and
volume less its openings), beams (`IfcBeam`), footings (`IfcFooting`), pipes (`IfcPipeSegment`), conduits, cable trays and wires (`IfcCableCarrierSegment`, `IfcCableSegment`) and structural columns and floors, each along
its own axis and, if structural, with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, the runs of a system assigned to an `IfcSystem` of its name, stairs and ramps as their flights, landings and railings (each railing with its
rail's top line as its axis), roofs as closed shells of flat faces (hip, gable, shed or flat), openings that cut the walls and hold the doors and windows, an opening for each slab, ceiling and roof a shaft passes
through, masses as building element proxies of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set), and components as furniture, sanitary or waste terminals, pipe fittings, valves, distribution boards, outlets,
switching devices, communications appliances, light fixtures or proxies, named `Family:Type` as Revit names them, each form a closed face set in its material's colour, each element's values of the project parameters in a
`Project Parameters` property set (dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations belong to views, and stay out of it), and each element's phase and design option in a `BIMCraft_Phasing` property set: its `Phase Created` is
always named in it, the first phase too (said to be implied, for another tool to read; a door or window says only what it holds, as one with no phase follows its wall), `Phase Demolished` and `Design Option` where it
holds them, and the project's phases in order, with the phase filters, overrides and option sets it changed, in one on the project, and, as IFC says it, its `Status` in its `Pset_*Common` (`EXISTING`, `DEMOLISH`, `NEW`
or `TEMPORARY`, for another tool to filter the work by); a project that uses none of it writes none |
-----

corner, a line's or a grid's end), which a square marks, then click away from them where the dimension line goes; more picks make a chain. Linear: pick endpoints, then click where it goes, horizontal or vertical as the
cursor lies; the Options Bar's Place (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them) lays either tool's dimension. Angular: pick two lines that meet, then click where the arc goes; the angle on that side. Radial
and Diameter: pick a round column, a curved wall, a circle or an arc, then click where it goes. Arc Length: pick a curved wall or an arc, then, to measure part of it, two ends on it, then click where the dimension's arc
goes. Edit Type on a dimension opens Dimension Type Properties; a double click on one of its numbers opens Dimension Text, that segment's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, or text in its place. Selected, a
dimension shows a padlock under each segment and EQ past its end: a click locks a segment at its length, or keeps the segments equal, and what it measures to then moves with what moves, as in Revit. Annotate > Tag by
Category (TG): click any element with a place in a plan (a door or window, a wall, a column, a component, a floor, ceiling or roof, a room, a beam or pipe, a stair) to tag it with its type, a door's or window's with its
mark, a room's with its name, or with any other field its schedule has (Height, Area, a project parameter) typed in Label in the Options Bar, with a leader when it says so; Tag All tags the doors and windows of the view
not tagged yet. Drag a dimension or a tag to move it |
-----
378 | Spot elevations, text | Annotate > Spot Elevation (EL): click a floor, a roof, a stair or a wall in plan, and it reads the height of its top there, following it; in a section, click a point to mark its height. Annotate
> Text (TX): type the note in the Options Bar (`\n` breaks a line), then click its top left corner, in a plan, a section or on a sheet; Properties sets its size and angle |
-----
379 | Crop, view range | View > Crop View crops a plan or a section to what it shows; drag the grips at its edges' middles to move them (a section's sides move its line). Off shows it all again: a section or an elevation,
all there is along its line, past its ends. Properties of a plan holds its View Range: Top (clear it for the level above), Cut Plane, Bottom and View Depth, in mm above the level |
-----
380 | Filled regions | Annotate > Filled Region (FR) and Masking Region start a boundary sketch. Edit Type opens Type Properties for a selected region or the current sketch: duplicate and rename types; choose foreground and
background patterns and colors separately; set masking; check the combined preview. A pattern's … button opens the patterns, to create and edit them. Apply/OK save the draft as one undo step; Cancel drops unapplied work.
A type change updates every region using it; the palette's Type Selector controls the instance's type. Non-masking fills keep cut foreground patterns and projected model lines visible; masking fills cover the model.
Sketches snap to visible model edges, detail lines, existing region boundaries and their own geometry, with the configured snaps and angle guides. |
-----
381 | Visibility/Graphics | View > Visibility/Graphics (VV, VG) opens the active view's dialog, a table as Revit's: a row for each model category (searched by name, with All, None and Invert, and Object Styles… for what
isn't overridden), its visibility, then Projection/Surface Lines, Patterns and Transparency, Cut Lines and Patterns, each cell showing what it overrides (the line as it draws, the fill's colour, the percent) and opening
its own small dialog (lines: a colour, weight and dash, each with a box that turns it on; patterns: a fill colour; transparency, seen in 3D; Clear Overrides), Halftone a box in the row, and Detail Level, By View until a
category can have its own; the Annotation Categories have their lines and halftone; Filters applies the project's filters in order, each a row alike, with Add, Remove, Up and Down; Elements lists what's hidden or
overridden one by one. Design Options picks which option of each set the view shows (the primary unless it chooses). OK and Apply send what changed as one `graphics` command, one undo step; Cancel drops it. A view that
follows a view template shows what the template controls, and leaves it be |
-----
382 | Hide in View | Select, then Modify > View: Hide Element (EH) leaves the elements out of the view, Hide Category (VH) every category the selection is of, Override Graphics (EO) opens Visibility/Graphics on its Elements
tab with the selection added. Unhide Elements (EU) opens that tab, with what's hidden; tick a box to bring it back |
-----
383 | Temporary hide and isolate | The view control bar under a plan, a section or the 3D view: Temporary Hide/Isolate hides the selected elements (HH) or their categories (HC), or isolates them (HI) or their categories
(IC), in that view only, and Reset (HR) brings it all back; the view wears a cyan frame meanwhile. The four hide and isolate items are greyed out until something is selected, as in Revit. Apply Hide/Isolate to View makes
it the view's own, as one undo step. Reveal Hidden Elements (RH) draws what the view hides for good in magenta, and again hides it. None of this is saved or undone: it is the window's |
-----
384 | Scale, detail level, visual style | The view control bar's first buttons. In a plan, a section or an elevation, Scale lists 1 : 1 to 1 : 1000, or in a project in feet and inches the architect's scales (12" = 1'-0" to
1/32" = 1'-0") and the engineer's (1" = 10'-0" to 1" = 200'-0"), and takes any other typed in Custom, as n, 1 : n or `1/4" = 1'-0"` (every view has one: 1 : 100, or 1/8" = 1'-0" in feet and inches, until it is given
another, and its annotation and line weights are the paper's at that scale); Detail Level picks Coarse, Medium or Fine. In the 3D view, Visual Style picks Shaded, Hidden Line or Wireframe; WF, HL and SD do too, as in
Revit. Its menu ends with Graphic Display Options (GD, as Revit's): Show Edges, Silhouettes (none, or an outline 1 to 10 px wide round what stands against what is behind) and Show Ambient Shadows (soft shadows where
faces meet), drawn alike on the processor and on the graphics card. Each is one undo step, saved with the project, and in a sheet's viewport the view draws as it says. A view's Properties have the same: View Scale (the
scales the Scale menu lists), Scale Value 1: (a typed scale) and Detail Level, or in the 3D view Visual Style. A view that follows a view template that controls one shows the template's value, greyed out, with the
template's name on hover |
-----
385 | Filters, view templates | View > Filters (FT): New makes a view filter; tick its categories and add rules as a schedule's filter has them. View > View Templates (VT), as Revit's: the templates on the left, on a tab for
each kind of view (Plan, Elevation/Section, 3D), with New from This View (a template of the view open), Duplicate, Rename and Delete under them; on the right the one picked, a table of Parameter, Value and Include: its
view scale, detail level and visual style, its V/G Overrides, V/G Filters and Design Options (Visibility/Graphics on the template), its view range, phase and phase filter, its background grids, each ticked under Include
for the views following it to take. OK and Apply send each template's changes as one command; Cancel drops them. A view's Properties name its template on a button that opens the same dialog, <None> first, to pick the one
it follows |
-----
386 | Phasing | Manage > Phasing (PH). Project Phasing lists the phases in order: type a name and Add at End, Insert Before or Insert After the one picked, Rename it, or Combine with Previous or Next, which takes it out and
gives what was made, taken down and shown in it to its neighbour. Phase Filters picks a filter (New Filter makes one) and sets how it shows each of New, Existing, Demolished and Temporary: By Category, Overridden or Not
Displayed. Graphic Overrides edits how each status draws where a filter says Overridden, and Apply Overrides sends it as one command. A view's Phasing group in Properties holds its Phase Filter and its Phase (the last
unless one is picked); a selected element's holds Phase Created and Phase Demolished, and its Design Option once the project has any |
-----
387 | Demolish | Modify > Phasing > Demolish (DW), then click an element in a plan, a section or the 3D view: its `Phase Demolished` becomes the view's phase (the project's last unless the view has one), as one undo step,
and it shows demolished there by the view's phase filter. Click it again, and it comes back. A door or window with no phase of its own comes down with its wall without being touched, and a click on it says so; something
that holds no parameters, such as a dimension, says so and stays as it was. The tool stays on until Esc |
-----
388 | Design options | Manage > Design Options (DO): New Set (with a name typed) makes a set with one option; pick an option and Add Option, Rename Option, Make Primary or Delete Option, or Edit Option, which makes it the
active one. Accept Primary keeps the primary's elements and takes the others' and the set away; Delete Set takes the set with every element in its options. The status bar's Active design option (once there are sets) is
what new elements are made in, Main Model for none, and the view on screen shows it too; it turns red in a view that shows another option of its set, and picking it again shows it there |
-----
389 | Lengths | While a tool waits for its next point, type a length and press Enter: it goes that far toward the cursor. A selected wall shows its length as a temporary dimension, and a selected door or window two, to its
middle from the faces of the walls meeting its wall either side of it (or its wall's ends); a selected column, structural column, footing or component shows how far it stands from the nearest wall centre line or grid
east, north, west and south, and the Column and Component tools sketch the same before the click; click a number to type a new one (the wall's end moves, the opening slides along its wall, the column or component moves)
|
-----
390 | Snaps and the ruler | While a tool picks points, what a click would land on is marked: a square for an end, a triangle for a middle, a cross for a crossing, a circle for a centre, a right angle for a perpendicular, a
diamond for the nearest point of a wall, a dot on an angle guide, each named beside it. Past the last point a dashed guide runs at the angle the direction sticks to (from east, and from the line before), and the new line
wears a ruler: its length and angle read beside it, and at a corner the angle between the two walls, shown as an arc, so a 60° corner is easy to hit. Shift keeps a step square. Manage > Snaps turns each snap off, and
sets the angle steps or turns them off; typed over the plan, SE, SM, SI, SC, SP or SN snap to endpoints, midpoints, intersections, centres, perpendiculars or the nearest point alone for the next point, SO to nothing, and
SS puts the snaps back (the status bar says which is waiting; a click, Esc, another tool or another view ends it) |
-----
391 | Measure | Annotate > Measure (ME): click two points; a ruler with its graduations lies between them, reading its length, its angle and its parts along x and y. Esc takes the ruler away, then the tool |
-----
392 | Turn a wall's points | Select one wall: a grip stands at each end. Drag one to move that end: its angle and length follow the cursor, with the snaps and angle guides from the other end, and the walls joined there
follow; Ctrl keeps the wall's length, so it turns about its other end. Beside each end is the wall's angle: click it and type a new one, and the wall turns about that end (a wall joined at its other end stays joined, the
corner sliding along the wall it meets) |
-----
393 | Edit types | Edit Type opens Type Properties, one dialog for every kind of type, as Revit's: the family and the type at the top with Duplicate and Rename, the type's parameters in a table under group bars that fold
(Construction, Dimensions, Materials and Finishes, Graphics, Text…), and OK, Cancel and Apply. Change the type everywhere it's used, Duplicate it into a new one, or Rename it (what's of it follows). A wall type's layers,
from the exterior in, or a floor's, roof's or ceiling's, from the top down: each one's function, material and thickness; Insert Layer, and Out and In (Up and Down) and Delete on each |
-----
394 | Place components | Component (CM): pick a family's type in the Type Selector, or in the Project Browser's Families, then click where it goes; Space turns it a quarter turn first. Selected, its own parameters are in
Properties, its type's in Type Properties (Edit Type), with Duplicate. Load Family, on Modify \| Place Component, loads a family saved as .json. A door's or a window's family is picked in the Type Selector of the Door or
Window tool, or of a selected door or window, as `Family: Type` beside the project's own types, which a new door takes from the project's single door or fixed window; its Edit Type is the family type's |
-----
395 | Family Editor | Manage > New Family (a category's template) and Edit Family (the family of what's selected, or of the component being placed): the family's name and category; Parameters (name, kind, instance, value,
formula); Types (a name and the type parameters' values, a blank one the family's own; add, duplicate, delete); Forms (a profile's corners, a circle, a revolve's axis and degrees, a void, its plane, from and to, material
and the parameter or formula it's visible by; moved up and down, deleted; Add Box, Cylinder, Revolve, Void); Symbols for a door or window. A preview of the type picked, turned by dragging. Apply makes the project's
family what's typed, one undo step; OK also closes; Save Family writes a `.json` file; Load Family reads one; Add to Favorites keeps it in your Favorites |
-----
396 | Favorites | Manage > Favorites: the materials and families you keep for every project, listed with a swatch; Add to Project (under another name when the project has that one) and Remove. A material comes in with the
picture its texture is made of, a family with the materials it's made of |
-----
397 | Paint | Modify > Paint (PT), in the 3D view: pick the material in the Options Bar, then click a face; Remove Paint takes it off the face clicked |
-----
398 | Materials | Manage > Materials: the project's library. Pick a material, or New for another, and set its name, colour, cut pattern and surface pattern; Delete takes one out that no layer uses. A layer picks its material
from the library. Texture picks a pattern drawn in code, or Picture… a PNG or JPEG file from your disk, for the 3D view; its tile's width and height, angle and offset follow; Save to Favorites keeps the material, and
Favorites… opens them |
-----
399 | Project parameters | Manage > Project Parameters: New makes one; name it, choose its type of parameter (text, number, length or yes/no) and the categories it's for. Select an element and its values are under Project
Parameters in Properties; empty a field to take a value away |
-----
491 | `reinforcement_preset` | | `name?`, `kind?` (beam, column, footing, floor), `params?` (what `reinforce` takes, but the host), `rename?`, `delete?`: a named set of parameters, kept in the project; no `name` lists them |
-----
534 | `phase` | | `name?`, `before?` or `after?` (to add one in place), `rename?`, `delete?` with `into?` (the phase that takes what was in it), `now?` (the phase this session makes elements in), `overrides?` ({`new`,
`existing`, `demolished` or `temporary`: an override, null takes it away}): the project's phases in order, and how a phase filter draws a status it says overridden. An element is made in a phase by its `Phase Created`
parameter and taken down in one by `Phase Demolished` (`modify {params}`) |
-----
535 | `phase_filter` | | `name`, `new?`, `existing?`, `demolished?`, `temporary?` (`by-category`, `overridden` or `not-displayed`), `delete?`: how a view shows each status of what is in its phase; a view applies one with
`graphics {phase_filter}` |
-----
536 | `option` | | `set?`, `options?` ([names]), `primary?`, `option?`, `rename?`, `delete?`, `accept?`, `now?` (`set: option`, or null: the option this session makes elements in): sets of design options; an element is in
one by its `Design Option` parameter, and a view chooses which to show with `graphics {options}` |
-----
537 | `level` | LL | `elevation`, `name?`, `extent?` [[x,y],[x,y]] |
-----
538 | `measure` | ME | `from`, `to` (points, mm): what a ruler laid between them reads: `length`, `dx`, `dy`, and `angle` in degrees from east, counter-clockwise; it changes nothing |
-----
539 | `line_weights` | | `model?` ([{`scale`, `widths`: the 16 pens' widths, mm}, …]), `annotation?` (the 16 pens' widths), `reset?`: the project's Line Weights, each pen's width on paper: the model's at each scale (a view
takes the nearest scale's), the annotation's at any; pen 0 is always a hairline; without any, what they are |
-----
540 | `object_styles` | | `categories?` ({category: {`projection?`, `cut?`}: pens 0 to 16}), `reset?`: the project's Object Styles, the pen each model category draws its own lines in, seen and cut, in every plan and section,
under a view's Visibility/Graphics; without either, each category's |
-----
541 | `line_pattern` | | `name?`, `segments?` (1–32 freely ordered Gap/`space`, Straight/`dash`, `dot_length`, `offset`, `wave`, `zigzag`, `text` segments; lengths in paper mm), `rename?`, `delete?`: create/edit a graphic
line pattern. Offset has `length`, `count` (2–9), `distance`; waves/zigzags have `length`, `frequency` (cycles per segment), `amplitude`; text has `length`, `size`, `text`, in bundled IBM Plex Sans, flowing along curves.
Geometry and dimensions retain the centerline. Without a name, lists every pattern |
-----
542 | `line_style` | | `name?`, `pen?` (0 to 16), `color?`, `pattern?` (a line pattern's name, or `Solid`), `rename?`, `delete?`: a line style of the project's, what detail lines draw in; without `name`, every one |
-----
543 | `fill_pattern` | | `name?`, `target?` (drafting, mm on paper; model, mm in the building), `lines?` ([{`angle`, `spacing`, `origin?`, `shift?`, `dashes?`}, …]; none, solid), `rename?`, `delete?`: a fill pattern,
families of lines as a PAT file has them; without `name`, every pattern |
-----
544 | `filled_region_type` | | `name?`, `foreground?`, `foreground_color?`, `background?`, `background_color?`, `masking?`, `rename?`, `delete?`: a filled region type; without `name`, every type |
-----
545 | `import_fill_patterns` | | `path` or `text` (a PAT file), `replace?` (false): its patterns, in mm unless it says `;%UNITS=INCH`; one the project has is kept unless `replace`. At most 2,000 patterns are read; it returns
those `imported`, the first 100 `left_out` each with why, and `left_out_count` of them all |
-----
546 | `export_fill_patterns` | | `path?`, `names?`: the project's fill patterns as a PAT file, written to `path` or returned as `text` |
-----
547 | `filled_region` | FR | `sketch` (lines, any number of loops), `view?`, `type?` (Solid Black), `line_style?` (Thin Lines; null, invisible): a filled or masking region in one view, over model backgrounds (over the model
when masking) and under detail annotation; a non-masking one keeps the ink of the model in plans, elevations, sections and on sheets. Its sketch has to close; its model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by
`pattern_angle` (set with `modify`) |
-----
568 | `parameter` | | `name`, `kind?` (`text`, `number`, `length`, `yesno`), `categories?` (`wall`, `floor`, `ceiling`, `roof`, `door`, `window`, `room`, `column`, `structuralcolumn`, `footing`, `beam`, `stripfooting`,
`pipe`, `conduit`, `cabletray`, `wire`, `downconductor`, `groundconductor`, `cable`, `component`, `stair`, `ramp`, `railing`), `rename?`, `delete?`: a project parameter; an element of its categories holds a value of it
with `modify {id, params: {name: value}}` |
-----

# Phases and design options

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Phases (`Model::phases`, in order) and design options (`Model::option_sets`, `phasing.rs`) are values an element holds among its
`params`, under names no project parameter or family parameter may take (`phasing::CREATED`, `DEMOLISHED`, `OPTION`; `Phase Created` is the first
phase when it has no value, `Design Option` is `set: option`; `open` renames an older file's project parameter of such a name), so `modify`, copies, schedules (`From::Param` in `schedule::OWN`)
and view filters reach them as any other. `phasing::status` says what an element is at a phase's place in the order (new,
existing, demolished, temporary, or not there); a door or window with none of its own follows its wall (`phasing::value`), and
annotation, which holds no params, belongs to a view. A view's `Graphics` hold `phase` (the project's last unless it says),
`phase_filter` (every status by category unless it says; `Model::phase_filters` show each status by category, overridden or
not at all, and `Model::phase_overrides` draw the overridden ones, never hidden or see-through) and `options` (`{set: option}`,
a set's primary unless it says); `Look::of` hides what a phase, a filter or an option leaves out and paints what a filter
overrides, below the view's own overrides. `Session::phase` and `Session::option` are what commands make (`Session::stamp`
gives each new element its `Phase Created` (none for the first phase, but a door or window is named, or it would follow its
wall) and its `Design Option` where it holds none; a copy takes the session's and loses its `Phase Demolished`; `split`, undo,
redo and the commands that replace the project stamp nothing); a refused command leaves them as they were; they
belong to the session, not the model, and the desktop sets them before each command (`BimApp::made_in`): the phase of the view
on screen when it has a phase or a phase filter of its own, and the active design option (`activate`, which shows it in the
view too). What was made in the first phase holds no value, so a phase put in before the first, or the first deleted, names it first
(`phasing::pin_first`; a door or window follows its wall, which is named). Deleting or combining a phase moves what was in it to
`into` (`phasing::move_phase`), and renaming a phase, an option or a set takes the elements, the views and the rules of filters
and schedules along; accepting a set keeps the primary's elements and deletes the rest.
IFC carries them in property sets named `ifc::PHASING`, `BIMCraft_Phasing`. An element that holds a phase or an option gets one:
`Phase Created` (always: the first phase is named too, with `ifc::IMPLIED` as its description where the element holds none, but a
door or window holds only what it says, or one with no phase would stop following its wall), `Phase Demolished` and `Design
Option`, as text. The project gets one when an element holds a phase or an option, or it changed its phases, filters or overrides,
or has an option set: `Phases`, a list of the names in order, and, where it changed them, `Phase Filters`, `Phase Overrides` and
`Design Option Sets` as the JSON a project file holds them in; a project that uses none of it writes none, and the file is as it
was. A phased project also says, for any tool that reads IFC's own words, what the work does to each element: `Status`
(`ifc::ifc_status`) in its `Pset_*Common` (`ifc::common_pset`, the one set that holds `LoadBearing` too), `DEMOLISH` where it is
taken down, `TEMPORARY` where that is in the phase it was made in, `EXISTING` where it was made in the first phase and `NEW`
else; a door or window with no phase says its wall's. It is written, not read: the import still takes phases from `BIMCraft_Phasing`. `import.rs` reads them beside the project parameters: what the project can't have (a phase or an option it hasn't, a
demolition before the creation, a list or a JSON that breaks `phasing::check_project`) is left out and listed, and the element
stays (it is the property, not the element, that breaks the rule); an implied `Phase Created` is no value; no other set is read, so
one another tool writes for phases, `Phasing` say, changes nothing.
A schedule sorts and groups `Phase Created` and `Phase Demolished` by the phase's place in `Model::phases`, not by its name, no
`Phase Demolished` coming after every phase (`schedule::sorts_as`); its filters still compare the names. The desktop's Demolish
tool (DW, `BimApp::demolish`, in the Modify tab's Phasing panel) runs `modify {params: {Phase Demolished}}` on the element clicked in a
plan, a section or the 3D view: the phase of the view on screen (the project's last unless it has one), or null when the element
already comes down in it, one undo step a click. A door or window that only follows its wall gets a note instead, and an element that
holds no `params` (annotation, levels, grids, shafts) says so and changes nothing.
The view control bar's Renovation menu (`BimApp::renovation_menu`, `phasing.rs` in the desktop, the same in both profiles) says in plain
words which phase of the work a plan, a section or the 3D view shows: All (no phase and no phase filter of its own, the view as it
starts), Existing (the project's first phase, every status by its category), Demolition (the last phase through a filter that hides
what is new, draws what stood before by its category and what comes down overridden) and New (the last through one that draws what
stood before overridden and hides what comes down). A pick is one `graphics {phase, phase_filter}`, one undo step. The words map onto
filters by what they do, never by their names, which a project renames or has in its own language (`RENOVATION`, `renovation`,
`filter_for`): the project's `Show Previous + Demolished` and `Show Previous + New` to start with. A choice the project has no
filter for is greyed out and says so, a view whose phase and filter match none of them shows Custom, the menu is greyed out where
a view template sets the phase, and the Sketch scale leaves it out with the rest of phasing.

for cmd in a:
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='h')
    args = [exe, 'run']
    for p in pre: args += ['--cmd', p]
    args += ['--cmd', cmd, '--cmd', 'inspect']
    p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    lines = p.stdout.decode('utf-8', 'replace').strip().split('\n')
    h = None
    try:
        h = json.loads(lines[-1])['history']
    except Exception:

    reply = lines[len(pre)] if len(lines) > len(pre) else ''

reinforce | {host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover short of its outline and its openings; a sloped floor's bars follow its top, the cover square to it. The bars are `rebar` elements of the host, each on a `layer`; reinforcing again replaces the ones it made and leaves any drawn by hand. `check` "NBR 6118" (with `aggressiveness` 1 to 4 for the cover, and `fck` in MPa) adds `notes` to the reply where the bars made fall short of that standard's usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars): they are notes, ne

tag | {ids?: [id,…], label?, level?, category?, offset?: [dx, dy], leader?} tags elements with a field of theirs: a door's or window's mark, a room's name, else the type, or `label`, any field its category's schedule has (`Height`, `Area`, a project parameter); doors, windows, walls, columns, components, floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms, runs and stairs. `offset` mm from the point it names (beside the wall for a door or window, else up and right); without ids, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`

family | {name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. rebar | {points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. wire | {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

cabling | {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to

A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. import subprocess, sys, tempfile, json
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
def ok(ll, ln):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    args = [ORIG, 'run', '--cmd', 'voltage {"name":"N","nominal":%r}' % ln, '--cmd', 'voltage {"name":"L","nominal":%r}' % ll,
            '--cmd', 'distribution_system {"name":"X","phases":3,"wires":4,"l_l":"L","l_n":"N"}']
    p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    return p.returncode == 0, p.stderr.decode().strip()
mode = sys.argv[1]
if mode == 'scan':
    ln = float(sys.argv[2])
    for ll in [float(x) for x in sys.argv[3:]]:
        print(ll, ll / ln, ok(ll, ln))
elif mode == 'bisect':
    ln = float(sys.argv[2]); lo = float(sys.argv[3]); hi = float(sys.argv[4])
    # lo is ok, hi not ok (or vice versa)
    a = ok(lo, ln)[0]; b = ok(hi, ln)[0]
    assert a != b, (a, b)
    for i in range(40):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        if ok(mid, ln)[0] == a: lo = mid
        else: hi = mid
    print('boundary between', lo, hi, 'ratio', lo / ln, hi / ln)

s = math.sqrt(3)
F = {

    'ii': lambda ll, ln: abs(ll - s * ln) / (s * ln) <= 0.03,
    'iii': lambda ll, ln: 0.97 < ll / (ln * s) < 1.03,
    'iv': lambda ll, ln: abs(ll / ln - s) <= 0.03 * s,
    'v': lambda ll, ln: abs(ll - s * ln) <= 0.03 * s * ln,
    'vi': lambda ll, ln: abs(ll / (s * ln) - 1) <= 0.03,
    'vii': lambda ll, ln: abs(ll / ln / s - 1.0) < 0.03,
}
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
def ok(ll, ln):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    args = [ORIG, 'run', '--cmd', 'voltage {"name":"N","nominal":%r}' % ln, '--cmd', 'voltage {"name":"L","nominal":%r}' % ll,
            '--cmd', 'distribution_system {"name":"X","phases":3,"wires":4,"l_l":"L","l_n":"N"}']

    return p.returncode == 0

import subprocess, json, sys
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
def run(cmds):
    args = [ORIG, 'run']
    for c in cmds: args += ['--cmd', c]
    p = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, cwd='/tmp')
    return p.stdout.decode().strip(), p.stderr.decode().strip()
sched = {}
cats = ['wall', 'floor', 'ceiling', 'roof', 'door', 'window', 'room', 'column', 'component', 'stair', 'ramp', 'railing', 'mass',
        'structuralcolumn', 'footing', 'beam', 'stripfooting', 'pipe', 'duct', 'conduit', 'cabletray', 'wire', 'downconductor',
        'groundconductor', 'cable']
for c in cats:
    o, e = run(['schedule ' + json.dumps({"name": "S", "category": c})])
    sched[c] = json.loads(o)['available']
allnames = sorted(set(n for v in sched.values() for n in v))
for c in cats:
    refused = []
    accepted = []
    msgs = set()
    for n in allnames:
        o, e = run(['parameter ' + json.dumps({"name": n, "categories": [c]})])
        if e:
            refused.append(n)
            m = e[e.find('`' + n + '`: ') + len(n) + 4:]
            msgs.add(m.replace(n, '<N>'))
        else:
            accepted.append(n)
    inlist = [n for n in refused if n in sched[c]]
    notinlist = [n for n in refused if n not in sched[c]]
    acc_in = [n for n in accepted if n in sched[c]]
    print(c, '| refused in avail:', inlist, '| refused not in avail:', notinlist, '| accepted though in avail:', acc_in)
    print('   msgs:', msgs)

"""Run cases through cmp.py. A case file has one case per line: commands separated by ' ;; '.
A line starting with 'FILE <path>' sets a project file opened first for the following cases (FILE - for none).
Each case runs: run [file] --cmd c1 --cmd c2 ... --cmd inspect? --save x.bimcraft
usage: batch.py casefile [-v]

import subprocess, sys, os
cmp = '/tmp/tools/cmp.py'

verbose = '-v' in sys.argv
nosave = '-n' in sys.argv
f = None
ok = bad = 0
for line in open(sys.argv[1]):
    line = line.rstrip('\n')
    if not line.strip() or line.startswith('#'):
        continue
    if line.startswith('FILE '):
        f = line[5:].strip()
        if f == '-': f = None
        continue
    cmds = [c.strip() for c in line.split(' ;; ')]
    args = ['python3', cmp]
    if f: args += ['-f', f]
    args += ['--', 'run']
    if f: args.append(os.path.basename(f))
    for c in cmds: args += ['--cmd', c]
    if not nosave: args += ['--save', 'x.bimcraft']

    if out.strip().endswith('SAME'):

        if verbose: print('SAME', line[:150])

content.text:
I implemented and tested `voltage`, `distribution_system`, `wire_type`, `reinforcement_preset` and `parameter` (with the checks they need and their `inspect` entries) in a private copy; every case I compared matches the original, except where the core is still missing pieces. Nothing in the worktree was touched and nothing is committed.

**Files to copy in** (all under `/tmp/styles-agent/elec/repo/src/styles/`):
- `electrical.rs`
- `presets.rs`
- `parameters.rs`

`parameters::check` also runs the preset and electrical checks, so `mod.rs` needs no change.

**What matches** (all checked with cmp.py, including the saved file and undo labels):
- **voltage**: 66 cases, all the same. Covers listing, show, create (the default band is ±10 % rounded to 0.1 V), change, rename and delete. Delete is refused while a distribution system uses the voltage.
- **distribution_system**: 81 cases, all the same. It stores voltages by GUID and shows them by name. Covered: the order of every check, the wires range for each phase count, and the 1.73 rule (within 3 % of √3).
- **wire_type**: 116 cases, all the same. That includes serde's exact errors for `sizes` (map keys read in sorted order; rows given as a list work), the 64-row cap, and row ordering.
- **reinforcement_preset**: 58 cases, all the same. Presets live in a top-level section `reinforcement`, which is dropped when it is empty. `params` are stored sorted, and only their names are checked against the kind.
- **parameter**: 174 cases, all the same, 68 of them on projects built with the original:
  - category names are normalised (any case, spaces/`_`/`-`, plurals, `masses`);
  - names are refused when malformed, reserved (Phase Created, Phase Demolished, Design Option, Paint, Mass Floor), one of the category's own fields, or a family parameter;
  - a kind change is refused while values exist;
  - a view filter with a rule on the parameter blocks delete or category removal;
  - removed categories strip element values and the matching schedule fields, filters and sorts.
- **Names given as GUIDs**: 37 cases, all the same. A GUID resolves to whatever library entry has it, of any kind. Only the hyphenated form counts, in any case, with or without braces.
- **Also the same**: undo and history sequences, other project languages, mixed sequences, and the inspect entries for voltages, distribution systems, wire types and parameters.
- **Model checks**: the messages match what the original shows when it opens a broken file. My check order is presets, voltages, distribution systems, wire types, parameter definitions, element values, then the "a name isn't a GUID" rule.

**What doesn't match**: only cases that need core pieces not yet in the repo: inspect output and core commands such as `beam`. One ordering gap: the original runs these checks before its level and grid checks, while `check.rs` runs `core_check` first. A file breaking both reports a different first error.

**Shared-file edits needed**
- `project.rs` `TOP_ORDER`: replace `"group_types", "reinforcement_presets"` with `"detail_groups", "reinforcement"`. The original's order is …, dimension_types, detail_groups, reinforcement, voltages, distribution_systems, wire_types, elements, library.
- `inspect.rs`: merge `crate::styles::inspect_entries(s)` into the reply. I did this in my copy to test it; it doesn't need copying from there.
- For your line styles: the original refuses any library name that looks like a GUID, e.g. "line style `…`: a name isn't a GUID; name it otherwise". You can reuse `electrical::check_guid_names(pr, kinds)` for your own kinds.

**What the core must provide**
- **Loading a file**:
  - If voltages, distribution systems or wire types are missing, fill in the defaults. If parameters is missing, use `{}`. Reuse library entries by name and create any that are missing.
  - Rename parameters with reserved names to "<name> Parameter" (then " 2" if that is taken). The open reply then carries a "renamed" map of old to new names.
  - Accept element `params` keyed by name and convert them to GUIDs.
  - Store numbers in these sections as floats (127 becomes 127.0).
  - Run the model check: errors read "open: <path>: <message>"; a missing field reads "<path> is not a BIMCraft project: missing field `max`".
- **`modify` and `elements`**: element `params` are keyed by the parameter's GUID (`parameters::key_of`, `param_of_key`, `for_category`).
  - My check produces "wall 100002: `X` isn't a parameter of walls; add it with `parameter`" and "`Len` holds a length, not "x"".
  - Values: numbers and lengths up to ±1e9, text up to 256 characters; null removes a value, and an empty `params` is dropped.
  - `elements` shows values by name.
- **Schedules and view filters** store project parameter fields by GUID, so a rename needs nothing.
- **Tags and calculated fields** name parameters by name. Their owners' checks refuse a rename that breaks them ("tag …: … has no field `…`", "schedule … calculated field …").
- **`reinforce {preset}`**: use `presets::find`. Its errors are "reinforce: there's no reinforcement preset `Nope`" and "reinforce: preset `C1` is for a column, and 100002 is a beam". Parameters given with the command replace the preset's.
- **Messages for other owners' checks**:
  - "`Paint` is {face: material}, not …"
  - "`Mass Floor` is {mass, level}, not …"
  - "`Phase Created` is one of the project's phases (…), not …"
